entries.name: Maximum groundspeed
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).

ambiguity.question: The limit is printed in two units that are not equal — 87 knots is 100.12 miles per hour — and the corpus does not say which governs, so a groundspeed above 100 mph and at or below 87 knots both exceeds and does not exceed it.

entries.note: The single figure, both units as printed: 87 knots / 100 mph. They differ by about 0.12 mph, and nothing in part 107 says the parenthetical is a rounding the knots figure overrides; that question is recorded rather than decided. Found by the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Maximum altitude above ground level
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: 400 feet, and the 400-foot structure radius and 400-foot above-structure allowance as three distinct figures.

entries.name: Minimum flight visibility
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.
entries.note: 3 statute miles, plus the section's own definition of flight visibility, which is a definition and not a threshold. The figure is fixed and this entry states it, which is why it stays clear; the definition it quotes turns on 'prominent', which the corpus never fixes, and that is prominent-objects — carried by the entry that applies the definition rather than by the one that states the figure.

entries.name: Minimum distance from clouds
entries.evidence: (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.

ambiguity.question: The two minimums are joined by "and" and no clearance above a cloud is stated. Read literally, the aircraft must be both at least 500 feet below and at least 2,000 feet horizontally from a cloud, which would bar flight level with or above a distant cloud; read as a region around the cloud, either distance suffices. The corpus does not say which.

entries.note: Both figures: 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal. A single combined value would lose the distinction. The figures are fixed; how they combine is not. Found by the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Civil twilight, outside Alaska
entries.evidence: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset;
entries.note: Both windows: 30 minutes before official sunrise to sunrise, and sunset to 30 minutes after.

entries.name: Groundspeed is within the limit
entries.evidence: (a) The groundspeed of the small unmanned aircraft may not exceed 87 knots (100 miles per hour).
entries.note: At, just below and just above 87 knots, and a groundspeed between 100 mph and 87 knots. Which printed figure governs is speed-limit's open question, reached through dependsOn.

entries.name: Altitude is within the limit
entries.evidence: (b) The altitude of the small unmanned aircraft cannot be higher than 400 feet above ground level, unless the small unmanned aircraft: (1) Is flown within a 400-foot radius of a structure; and (2) Does not fly higher than 400 feet above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.
entries.note: The plain 400 ft AGL case; inside a 400 ft radius of a structure; and the boundary where the aircraft is within the radius but above the structure's uppermost limit plus 400.

entries.name: Visibility and cloud clearance are met
entries.evidence: (c) The minimum flight visibility, as observed from the location of the control station must be no less than 3 statute miles. For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night. (d) The minimum distance of the small unmanned aircraft from clouds must be no less than: (1) 500 feet below the cloud; and (2) 2,000 feet horizontally from the cloud.
entries.note: Each minimum independently, and the case where one passes and the other fails. The cloud-clearance half has two stated figures, but whether both must hold at once or either suffices is cloud-clearance's open question. The visibility half is not: the quantity to be compared against 3 statute miles is the section's own 'flight visibility', whose definiens turns on which objects are 'prominent', and the corpus fixes no degree of prominence. That term is prominent-objects, split out rather than reclassifying this entry — classifying the whole entry by one of its clauses would have thrown away the 500-foot and 2,000-foot figures (0005).

entries.name: The operating limitations are complied with
entries.evidence: A remote pilot in command and the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system must comply with all of the following operating limitations when operating a small unmanned aircraft system:
entries.note: The lead-in of § 107.51: the four limitations are one obligation, and it binds both the remote pilot in command and the person manipulating the flight controls. No entry quoted it until the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)). Cases: all limitations met; each one failing; and each of the two named persons.

entries.name: Which objects are prominent, for flight visibility
entries.evidence: For purposes of this section, flight visibility means the average slant distance from the control station at which prominent unlighted objects may be seen and identified by day and prominent lighted objects may be seen and identified by night.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'prominent', and the term carries the whole visibility metric: the distance reported as flight visibility is the distance at which prominent objects can be seen, so the degree of prominence fixes the number that § 107.51(c)'s 3-statute-mile threshold is compared against.

entries.note: Gate 1 of 0008 passes: applying § 107.51(c) requires fixing a degree the corpus did not fix, which is what separates flight visibility from groundspeed — an ordinary caller-supplied parameter whose meaning is not open. Gate 2 does not fire: no corpus is named for it. Gate 3's first branch does not fire either — the clause states no measure for 'prominent' in its own constituent and names no decider — so the procedure returns a gap. The same shape as well-clear and moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area'. Found by the undefined-term sweep (#33, #34), not by inspection of the interesting entries.

entries.name: Only one aircraft is operated at a time
entries.evidence: A person may not manipulate flight controls or act as a remote pilot in command or visual observer in the operation of more than one unmanned aircraft at the same time.
entries.note: One aircraft; two aircraft; and the same person acting as visual observer for a second. The prohibition binds three roles — manipulating the flight controls, acting as remote pilot in command, acting as visual observer — and the evidence covers each.

entries.name: Controlled airspace requires prior ATC authorization
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in Class B, Class C, or Class D airspace or within the lateral boundaries of the surface area of Class E airspace designated for an airport unless that person has prior authorization from Air Traffic Control (ATC).
entries.note: Each of Class B, C, D and the lateral surface area of Class E, with and without authorization; and Class G, which needs none. The airspace class is an input. Determining it from a position requires a corpus this map has not admitted.

entries.name: Prohibited or restricted areas require permission
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft in prohibited or restricted areas unless that person has permission from the using or controlling agency, as appropriate.
entries.note: Both designations the section states — prohibited and restricted — with and without permission from the using or controlling agency. Same shape as airspace-authorized: the designation is an input, not something derived here.

entries.name: Operation from a moving land or water-borne vehicle
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system— ... (b) From a moving land or water-borne vehicle unless the small unmanned aircraft is flown over a sparsely populated area and is not transporting another person's property for compensation or hire.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'sparsely populated area', and the term carries the whole exception in (b).

entries.note: From a moving land or water-borne vehicle over a sparsely populated area without carriage for hire; and the two ways the exception fails. The summary an earlier note replaced said "a moving land vehicle" and dropped the water-borne case (#26). § 107.25(a), the moving-aircraft prohibition, was part of this entry and made ambiguous by (b)'s undefined term, which does not qualify it; it is moving-aircraft-operation since the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Operation from a moving aircraft
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system— (a) From a moving aircraft;
entries.note: A prohibition without exception: from a moving aircraft, and from an aircraft that is not moving. "Sparsely populated area" qualifies only (b). Split out of moving-vehicle-operation by the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Operation at night
entries.evidence: (a) Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section, no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system at night unless— (1) The remote pilot in command of the small unmanned aircraft has completed an initial knowledge test or training, as applicable, under § 107.65 after April 6, 2021; and (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.

crossReferences.cites: Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section

entries.note: Night with training and lighting; night without either; and the § 107.65 training date boundary of April 6, 2021. Whether lighting is fitted is computable; which training qualifies is night-training-completed's open question (found by the blind second mapping, blind-mapping/ (0014)); the sufficiency of the flash rate is asserted (flash-rate-sufficient) and so is the pilot's safety determination (intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety), both reached through anti-collision-lighting, whose locator cites the clause that states them. But the condition of application is "at night", and § 107.3 does not define night — it defines seven terms and night is not among them. § 107.3 puts § 1.1 of this chapter in force for this part ("if there is a conflict… the definitions in this part control"), so gate 2 of 0008 routes the term to definedElsewhere rather than to a gap, and the whole entry declines: without the term no case of § 107.29(a) is reachable, not even the case where it does not apply. That is why this is not split the way civil-twilight-alaska is — there two of the three limbs of civil twilight are fixed in the section itself, and there is a passage stating the deferral; here no passage states what night means. The limit, stated where the claim is: § 107.3's clause is a general priority rule and does not route this term to § 1.1 by name, so the claim that § 1.1 fixes it becomes checkable only when cfr-14-1 is admitted. The "Except as provided in paragraph (d)" carve-out resolves to night-waiver-bar, (d)'s first sentence, the one about operating at night (#28); (d)'s second sentence is night-waiver-termination. Both are scope: in rather than spent — see night-waiver-termination for why, and for the date this entry's earlier unmapped reason got wrong.

entries.name: The remote pilot in command has completed the knowledge test or training for night operation
entries.evidence: (1) The remote pilot in command of the small unmanned aircraft has completed an initial knowledge test or training, as applicable, under § 107.65 after April 6, 2021; and

ambiguity.question: Whether "initial" qualifies "training" as well as "knowledge test" is not settled, and "as applicable, under § 107.65" points at a section that names an initial aeronautical knowledge test (a), recurrent training (b) and training for part 61 certificate holders (c) without saying which satisfies § 107.29(a)(1); § 107.65(d) also treats some completions before April 6, 2021 as compliant with (b) or (c).

entries.note: The completion date against April 6, 2021 is computable once the qualifying completion is known; which completion qualifies is not. Split out of night-operation, which called the training condition computable, by the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Aeronautical knowledge recency
entries.evidence: A person may not exercise the privileges of a remote pilot in command with small UAS rating unless that person has accomplished one of the following in a manner acceptable to the Administrator within the previous 24 calendar months: (a) Passed an initial aeronautical knowledge test covering the areas of knowledge specified in § 107.73; (b) Completed recurrent training covering the areas of knowledge specified in § 107.73; or (c) If a person holds a pilot certificate (other than a student pilot certificate) issued under part 61 of this chapter and meets the flight review requirements specified in § 61.56, completed training covering the areas of knowledge specified in § 107.74. (d) A person who has passed a recurrent aeronautical knowledge test in a manner acceptable to the Administrator or who has satisfied the training requirement of paragraph (c) of this section prior to April 6, 2021 within the previous 24 calendar months is considered to be in compliance with the requirement of paragraph (b) or (c) of this section, as applicable.

crossReferences.unmapped: § 107.73 is outside this map's slice of twelve subpart B sections, and not needed to decline this one; no entry names it.

crossReferences.cites: issued under part 61 of this chapter and meets the flight review requirements specified in § 61.56
crossReferences.unmapped: 14 CFR part 61 is a corpus that was not admitted. This entry is scope: out and works nothing under (c), so there is no meaning of an in-scope rule for definedElsewhere to route; an out-of-scope entry answers its pointers into an unadmitted corpus here (0026, section 4).
§ 107.74 is outside this map's slice of twelve subpart B sections, and not needed to decline this one; no entry names it.
Paragraph (c) is quoted in this entry's own evidence.
Paragraphs (b) and (c) are quoted in this entry's own evidence.

entries.note: Out of scope: this map reads twelve sections of subpart B, and § 107.65 is not among them. It is an entry rather than an omission because § 107.29(a)(1) points at it ("as applicable, under § 107.65"), and which of (a)-(c), with (d)'s pre-2021 completions, satisfies that is night-training-completed's open question, which depends on this entry (0026). Nothing under the section is worked. The evidence is the whole section, so that the out-of-scope verdict covers each way of accomplishing recency. Added after the independent verdict on #116 found the pointer answered by an unmapped reason where 0026 asks for an entry.

entries.name: Termination of night waivers issued before March 16, 2021
entries.evidence: The certificates of waiver issued prior to March 16, 2021 under § 107.200 that authorize deviation from § 107.29 terminate on May 17, 2021.

crossReferences.unmapped: Identifies the terminated waivers by what they authorize deviation from. Whether a waiver does is a fact about the waiver the caller supplies, not a rule of this section evaluated through the pointer.

entries.note: § 107.29(a) opens "Except as provided in paragraph (d) of this section" and (d) had no entry in either direction (#28). It is an entry rather than an absence, and scope: in rather than out, because it is not spent. Both sentences are in force at this map's 2026-01-01 baseline: the first is a standing prohibition with no sunset — after May 17, 2021 no person may operate at night under a waiver issued before April 21, 2021 — and the second records a termination that has occurred. A rule whose condition can no longer be met is not a rule that is no longer in force, and method.md Phase 1 already draws that line: dates inside a rule are ordinary operations over a date the caller supplies, not corpus versioning. The temporal trial is the standing argument that such dates are answerable. The first sentence is night-waiver-bar since the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)): it turns on "at night", which this sentence does not, so only that one declines with night-operation. Cases here: a waiver issued before March 16, 2021, one issued between March 16 and April 21, 2021 (not terminated by this sentence), and the termination date itself. The map's earlier record of this carve-out, in night-operation's unmapped reason, said the waivers issued before March 16, 2021 "terminated on that date"; the text says they terminate on May 17, 2021 and March 16, 2021 is the issuance cut-off. Corrected here.

entries.name: No night operation after May 17, 2021 under a waiver issued before April 21, 2021
entries.evidence: (d) After May 17, 2021, no person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system at night in accordance with a certificate of waiver issued prior to April 21, 2021 under § 107.200.
entries.note: A standing prohibition with no sunset. Cases: a night operation after May 17, 2021 relying on a waiver issued before April 21, 2021; one relying on a later waiver; one relying on no waiver. "At night" is the term night-operation routes to § 1.1, and it is routed the same way here; the reference entry for (d) had no definedElsewhere until the blind second mapping (blind-mapping/ (0014)).

entries.name: Operation during civil twilight
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so. (c) For purposes of paragraph (b) of this section, civil twilight refers to the following: (1) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins 30 minutes before official sunrise and ends at official sunrise; (2) Except for Alaska, a period of time that begins at official sunset and ends 30 minutes after official sunset; and (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.

crossReferences.cites: as defined in the Air Almanac

entries.note: Inside and outside each twilight window, with and without lighting. Alaska is a separate entry: the corpus defers the definition elsewhere. It stays in dependsOn because (c)(3) is part of the definition of civil twilight this entry's rule turns on: without civil-twilight-alaska the entry cannot say whether an Alaskan operation is in civil twilight (blind-mapping/ (0014)). (c)'s "paragraph (b) of this section" resolves to anti-collision-lighting, whose locator cites § 107.29(a)(2) and (b) and whose evidence quotes all of (b) as amended by Amendment 107-8, both sentences; flash-rate-sufficient and intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety each quote one sentence of it. The pointer resolves to where (b) is stated; the rule that uses (c)'s definition is this entry's, and anti-collision-lighting does not depend on it. It was unmapped, with a reason saying no other entry states (b) whole, which was not true.

entries.name: Civil twilight in Alaska
entries.evidence: (3) In Alaska, the period of civil twilight as defined in the Air Almanac.
entries.note: § 107.29(c)(3) fixes the meaning of Alaskan civil twilight in the Air Almanac, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus is clear, and the text that would settle it is elsewhere. Nothing beyond the quoted sentence can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Carriage of hazardous material
entries.evidence: A small unmanned aircraft may not carry hazardous material. For purposes of this section, the term hazardous material is defined in 49 CFR 171.8.
entries.note: § 107.36 states the prohibition here and fixes the meaning of 'hazardous material' in 49 CFR 171.8, which this map has not admitted. Not an ambiguity: the corpus says exactly what it means and says where. Nothing beyond the quoted sentences can be evidenced from this corpus.

entries.name: Yielding right of way to other aircraft
entries.evidence: (a) Each small unmanned aircraft must yield the right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles. Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.
entries.note: Two enumerations, both computable: three protected kinds — aircraft, airborne vehicles, launch and reentry vehicles — and three prohibited relative positions — over, under, ahead. An engine told the object is none of the three, or that the manoeuvre is none of the three, decides the case without the open term at all, and the evidence covers each. The note this replaces said "nothing here is computed", which its own evidence contradicts (#34). What is not computed is the exception "unless well clear", which is well-clear and is a gap rather than an assertion: 0008 § 2 attacked the purpose clause at this joint and it gave way, so gate 3's first branch does not fire here.

entries.name: The small unmanned aircraft is well clear of the aircraft or vehicle
entries.evidence: Yielding the right of way means that the small unmanned aircraft must give way to the aircraft or vehicle and may not pass over, under, or ahead of it unless well clear.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define 'well clear', and the term carries the whole exception to the prohibition on passing over, under or ahead. 'Well clear' occurs exactly once in the corpus; § 107.3 does not define it and no other section does; and § 107.37(a) states no measure for it in its own constituent — 'must give way' is a coordinate obligation in the definiens, not what the clearance is measured against.

entries.note: Split out of right-of-way, which keeps the two computable enumerations (0005: a standard is its own entry, and the rule that consumes it depends on it). Not kind: assertion — gate 3's first branch requires the corpus to state, in the same constituent as the open term, either the measure or the set of values, and § 107.37(a) states neither. Not a value either: the corpus states no clearance. The kind records what the engine would have to do and cannot, which is why the entry declines at runtime rather than demanding a parameter. The same shape as moving-vehicle-operation's 'sparsely populated area', and the two now return the same answer, which they did not before. Where the project holds the term determinate — 'well clear' is a recognised operational standard in aviation practice — that is fate: decision with a record, never a kind (0008 § 3); this map does not hold it, so the fate is unresolved.

entries.name: Operating so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard
entries.evidence: (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft so close to another aircraft as to create a collision hazard.
entries.note: The corpus states a standard rather than a distance, deliberately, and § 107.37(b) is that sentence and nothing else — so the entry is reclassified in place rather than split. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. An engine that resolved it to a number would substitute its own rule for the corpus's. Who asserts it: § 107.37(b) names only the subject of the prohibition, "No person", and nobody whose determination settles the hazard, so assertedBy is the caller (0025).

entries.name: A covered structure or stationary vehicle provides reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft
entries.evidence: (b) That human being is located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft
entries.note: The standard qualifies the covered-structure exception; the exception itself is computable once it is asserted. The assertion is asserted and withheld for each of a covered structure and a stationary vehicle, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. Split out rather than reclassifying over-human-beings, which states two further cases that need no judgement. Who asserts it: § 107.39 names the subject of the prohibition, "No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being", and the human being protected, and nobody whose determination settles the protection, so assertedBy is the caller (0025).

entries.name: Operation over a human being
entries.evidence: No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft over a human being unless— (a) That human being is directly participating in the operation of the small unmanned aircraft; (b) That human being is located under a covered structure or inside a stationary vehicle that can provide reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft; or (c) The operation meets the requirements of at least one of the operational categories specified in subpart D of this part.
entries.note: Three causes, three entries. The undefined term in (a) is direct-participation, a gap — the exception turns entirely on it and the corpus states no measure (0010). The judgement in (b) is reasonable-protection, an assertion. The deferral in (c) is subpart-d-categories, which is scope: out and carries OutsideCurrentScope itself — a dependency, not a second reason on this entry. The evidence is the whole section: the participating-person case, both limbs of (b) — a covered structure and a stationary vehicle — and the subpart D case, plus a plain overflight with none of them.

entries.name: A human being is directly participating in the operation
entries.evidence: (a) That human being is directly participating in the operation of the small unmanned aircraft;

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "directly participating", and the term carries the whole of the § 107.39 exception it states: whether the aircraft may be flown over a person turns on it. "In the operation of the small unmanned aircraft" states what the participation is in, not how direct it must be, and no determination is vested in anybody.

entries.note: Gate 1 passes, gate 2 does not fire, and gate 3's first arm does not fire, so the procedure returns a gap. The same term delimits who must be briefed under § 107.49(b), and participant-briefing depends on this entry for that reason; the locator names § 107.39 alone because check-locators-section.py reads one section per citation, so an entry cannot cite two — a limit of the grammar rather than of the rule, stated where the claim is made. Compare § 107.39(b), whose "reasonable protection from a falling small unmanned aircraft" states its measure and is an assertion: two paragraphs of one sentence go opposite ways, and whose fact it is — a third party's, in both — is not what decides it. Found by 0010's re-derivation; trial 1's undefined-term sweep recorded this term against over-human-beings only and missed the § 107.49(b) instance.

entries.name: Operational categories for flight over human beings
entries.evidence: This subpart prescribes the eligibility and operating requirements for civil small unmanned aircraft to operate over human beings or over moving vehicles in the United States, in addition to those operations permitted by § 107.39(a) and (b).
entries.note: Out of scope for this trial, which maps subpart B only. Reachable from § 107.39(c), so an engine must be able to say OutsideCurrentScope rather than simply lacking it. Nothing under the subpart is worked; the evidence is the subpart's own applicability sentence, which is what makes the citation checkable at all.

entries.name: The anti-collision lighting has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision
entries.evidence: (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. ... (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision.
entries.note: The same clause qualifies the night requirement in (a)(2) and the civil-twilight requirement in (b), which is why it hangs off anti-collision-lighting — the entry whose locator cites both — rather than off night-operation alone. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent; the corpus states no rate, so no figure is evidenced. Added by Amendment 107-8; the 2020 text states no flash-rate requirement anywhere. Who asserts it: § 107.29(a) and (b) name the subject of the prohibition, "no person may operate", and nobody whose determination settles the flash rate; the remote pilot in command they name determines only whether to reduce the lighting's intensity, which is intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety. So assertedBy is the caller (0025).

entries.name: Reducing the anti-collision lighting intensity is in the interest of safety
entries.evidence: The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: The corpus delegates the judgement and names its decider in the same breath: "if he or she determines". § 107.29(a)(2) and (b) state the identical sentence, which is why the locator cites both and why the quoted evidence has two occurrences. The computable half stays where it was: the bound that intensity may be reduced but the lighting may not be extinguished is anti-collision-lighting's, and that entry depends on this one — the speed-limit / speed-within-limit shape 0005 names. This is the example method.md and corpus-map.md both cite for kind: assertion, and it had no entry of its own until #26.

entries.name: Anti-collision lighting is fitted and visible for 3 statute miles
entries.evidence: (2) The small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so. ... (b) No person may operate a small unmanned aircraft system during periods of civil twilight unless the small unmanned aircraft has lighted anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles that has a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. The remote pilot in command may reduce the intensity of, but may not extinguish, the anti-collision lighting if he or she determines that, because of operating conditions, it would be in the interest of safety to do so.
entries.note: Fitted and unfitted, for night and for civil twilight; the 3 statute mile visibility figure the corpus states plainly; and the bound the same clause states — the intensity may be reduced but the lighting may not be extinguished. Whether reducing it is in the interest of safety is the remote pilot in command's determination and is its own entry, intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety; the sufficiency of the flash rate is flash-rate-sufficient.

entries.name: Visual line of sight is maintained
entries.evidence: (a) With vision that is unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, the remote pilot in command, the visual observer (if one is used), and the person manipulating the flight control of the small unmanned aircraft system must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight in order to: (1) Know the unmanned aircraft's location; (2) Determine the unmanned aircraft's attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; (3) Observe the airspace for other air traffic or hazards; and (4) Determine that the unmanned aircraft does not endanger the life or property of another. (b) Throughout the entire flight of the small unmanned aircraft, the ability described in paragraph (a) of this section must be exercised by either: (1) The remote pilot in command and the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system; or (2) A visual observer.

crossReferences.cites: the ability described in paragraph (a) of this section

entries.note: (b) states the two permitted combinations and the evidence covers both: the remote pilot in command together with the person manipulating the flight controls, or a visual observer — and neither. Given the assertion, that is a membership test against a fixed pair of combinations, which is computable, and it is what survives the split. The note this replaces said "whether anyone could in fact see the aircraft is not computable. The engine demands the assertion and records who made it" while the entry stayed kind: operation, so the assertion it described was recorded nowhere. It is unaided-visual-contact, and this entry depends on it (0010).

entries.name: The aircraft can be seen unaided throughout the entire flight, for the four stated purposes
entries.evidence: (a) With vision that is unaided by any device other than corrective lenses, the remote pilot in command, the visual observer (if one is used), and the person manipulating the flight control of the small unmanned aircraft system must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight in order to: (1) Know the unmanned aircraft's location; (2) Determine the unmanned aircraft's attitude, altitude, and direction of flight; (3) Observe the airspace for other air traffic or hazards; and (4) Determine that the unmanned aircraft does not endanger the life or property of another.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires on the plainest measure in this corpus. § 107.31(a) states an open ability — "must be able to see the unmanned aircraft throughout the entire flight" — and fixes what it is measured against in the same constituent, with "in order to:" and four enumerated purposes. That is the "sufficient to avoid a collision" construction with four adjuncts instead of one. § 107.31(a)(4)'s "endanger the life or property of another" sits inside that measure and is not a second open term: § 107.31 does not prohibit endangering, it requires the ability to see well enough to determine. The assertion is asserted and withheld for each named person, attributed and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent; the corpus states no distance, so no figure is evidenced. Split out of visual-line-of-sight, which keeps § 107.31(b)'s two permitted combinations — 0005's rule that a standard is its own entry and the rule that consumes it depends on it. Decided in 0010.

entries.name: Visual observer requirements, when one is used
entries.evidence: If a visual observer is used during the aircraft operation, all of the following requirements must be met: (a) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must maintain effective communication with each other at all times. (b) The remote pilot in command must ensure that the visual observer is able to see the unmanned aircraft in the manner specified in § 107.31. (c) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must coordinate to do the following: (1) Scan the airspace where the small unmanned aircraft is operating for any potential collision hazard; and (2) Maintain awareness of the position of the small unmanned aircraft through direct visual observation.
entries.note: What survives the split is (b) and the condition of application: if a visual observer is used, the remote pilot in command must ensure the observer can see the aircraft in the manner § 107.31 specifies — computable once unaided-visual-contact is asserted, reached through visual-line-of-sight. (a) is effective-communication, a gap; (c) is observer-coordination, an assertion. The section's three requirements do not share one verdict, which is what 0010 decides. § 107.33(b)'s "in the manner specified in § 107.31" is declared in crossReferences and resolves to visual-line-of-sight, the entry that states § 107.31 whole; it is the same edge as dependsOn. An earlier sentence here said the words were outside check-map.py's pointer list and nothing demanded a declaration; the manifest's pointerPhrases now detect "§ 107.31" (0026), so that was no longer true.

entries.name: Effective communication is maintained among the three named persons
entries.evidence: (a) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must maintain effective communication with each other at all times.

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "effective", and the term carries the whole of § 107.33(a). The paragraph states no measure for it in its own constituent — "with each other at all times" fixes between whom and when, not what effectiveness is measured against — and vests the determination in nobody: it is an obligation on three named persons, not a judgement the corpus gives them.

entries.note: Gate 1 passes: applying the paragraph requires fixing a degree the corpus did not fix. Gate 2 does not fire — § 107.3 does not define the term and no corpus is named for it. Gate 3's first arm does not fire, so the procedure returns a gap: the same shape as well-clear, prominent-objects and moving-vehicle-operation's "sparsely populated area". That the operator is the only person who could answer the question is not what gate 3 asks. An operator who asserts that communication was effective has asserted a conclusion the engine cannot check and that the corpus gave it no warrant to delegate; 0008 § 2 rules that where a term's determinacy rests on knowledge outside the corpus, that belief is fate: decision with a record, never a kind. Split out of visual-observer-conditions (0010).

entries.name: The three named persons coordinate to scan the airspace and maintain awareness
entries.evidence: (c) The remote pilot in command, the person manipulating the flight controls of the small unmanned aircraft system, and the visual observer must coordinate to do the following: (1) Scan the airspace where the small unmanned aircraft is operating for any potential collision hazard; and (2) Maintain awareness of the position of the small unmanned aircraft through direct visual observation.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires: "must coordinate" is followed in the same constituent by "to do the following:" and a closed two-item enumeration — scan the airspace for any potential collision hazard, and maintain awareness of the position through direct visual observation. The infinitival adjunct states what the coordination is for exactly as "to avoid a collision" states what the flash rate is for. "Maintain awareness" is inside that enumeration and is not a second open term, and "through direct visual observation" fixes its means. The assertion is asserted and withheld, attributed to the three named persons and recorded with the outcome, and never defaulted to true when absent. Split out of visual-observer-conditions (0010).

entries.name: Preflight familiarization, inspection and actions
entries.evidence: Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must: (a) Assess the operating environment, considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air. This assessment must include: (1) Local weather conditions; (2) Local airspace and any flight restrictions; (3) The location of persons and property on the surface; and (4) Other ground hazards. (b) Ensure that all persons directly participating in the small unmanned aircraft operation are informed about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards; (c) Ensure that all control links between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly; (d) If the small unmanned aircraft is powered, ensure that there is enough available power for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time; (e) Ensure that any object attached or carried by the small unmanned aircraft is secure and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft; and (f) If the operation will be conducted over human beings under subpart D of this part, ensure that the aircraft meets the requirements of § 107.110, § 107.120(a), § 107.130(a), or § 107.140, as applicable.

crossReferences.cites: under subpart D of this part

entries.note: Six obligations in this text, and they do not share one verdict: (a), (b) and (d) are assertions, (c) is a gap, and (e) is one of each — preflight-risk-assessment, participant-briefing, control-links-working, sufficient-available-power, attached-object-secure and attached-object-no-adverse-effect. The note this replaces said "Six obligations, all assertions about what a person did", which is wrong twice over: three of them are about equipment rather than conduct, and two state no measure at all and are gaps (0010). Each obligation asserted and unasserted. What is left here is the conjunction — prior to flight the remote pilot in command must do all of them — plus (f), which is reachable only through subpart D and is a dependency on subpart-d-categories rather than a second reason on this entry.

entries.name: The operating environment has been assessed against the stated risks
entries.evidence: (a) Assess the operating environment, considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air. This assessment must include: (1) Local weather conditions; (2) Local airspace and any flight restrictions; (3) The location of persons and property on the surface; and (4) Other ground hazards.
entries.note: Gate 3's first arm fires twice over: "Assess the operating environment" is qualified in its own constituent by "considering risks to persons and property in the immediate vicinity both on the surface and in the air" — what the assessment is measured against — and then by a closed four-item list of what it must include. The bearer is named in the section's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:", and is who asserts it (assertedBy, 0025). The limit, stated where the claim is made: the measure itself carries an open degree, "immediate vicinity", and gate 3 does not ask whether a stated measure is itself determinate. A measure that needs a measure is a shape 0008's procedure cannot see; 0010 records it rather than deciding it.

entries.name: The directly participating persons have been informed of the five stated matters
entries.evidence: (b) Ensure that all persons directly participating in the small unmanned aircraft operation are informed about the operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards;
entries.note: "Informed about" is fixed by the set stated in the same constituent — operating conditions, emergency procedures, contingency procedures, roles and responsibilities, and potential hazards — which is gate 3's second arm, the delegated choice among values the corpus fixes ("either thrice or four times"), and the set is quotable from this entry's own evidence. The audience is not fixed: "all persons directly participating" is the same undefined term as § 107.39(a), which is direct-participation, a gap, and this entry depends on it. One paragraph, two open terms, two verdicts — which is the sharpest instance of what 0010 decides. Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: The control links are working properly
entries.evidence: (c) Ensure that all control links between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft are working properly;

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "working properly", and the term carries the whole obligation. § 107.49(c) states no measure for it in its own constituent — "between ground control station and the small unmanned aircraft" identifies which links, not what properly is measured against — and vests the determination in nobody.

entries.note: Gate 3 returns a gap, the same answer as effective-communication, prominent-objects and well-clear. That the remote pilot in command is the only person who could answer it is not gate 3's question (0008 § 2). Split out of preflight-actions (0010).

entries.name: There is enough available power for the intended operational time
entries.evidence: (d) If the small unmanned aircraft is powered, ensure that there is enough available power for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time;
entries.note: "Enough available power" is followed in its own constituent by "for the small unmanned aircraft system to operate for the intended operational time" — an infinitival adjunct on enough, the same construction as "a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision". Gate 3's first arm fires. The intended operational time is an ordinary caller-supplied parameter that gate 1 stops and that gets no entry of its own, as corpus-map.md rules for airspace-authorized's airspace class. Split out of preflight-actions (0010). Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: An attached or carried object is secure
entries.evidence: Ensure that any object attached or carried by the small unmanned aircraft is secure

ambiguity.question: Part 107 does not define "secure", and § 107.49(e) states no measure for it. The second conjunct — "and does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft" — is a coordinate predicate of the same copula, not the measure of the first.

entries.note: 0008 § 2 rules that a coordinate conjunct is a second obligation rather than a measure, which is exactly how "must give way" was refused as the measure of "well clear". So § 107.49(e) is two entries with opposite verdicts, this one and attached-object-no-adverse-effect. The limit, stated where the claim is made: a reader could take the second conjunct as a gloss on the first — secure enough not to affect the flight — and 0005 refused to put one sentence under two ids when it declined to split must-play-whole-throw. The nearer precedent is followed instead: right-of-way and well-clear are one sentence under two ids for precisely this reason (0010).

entries.name: An attached or carried object does not adversely affect flight characteristics or controllability
entries.evidence: does not adversely affect the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft
entries.note: "Adversely affect" states what it is measured against in its own constituent and enumerates it: the flight characteristics or controllability of the aircraft. Gate 3's first arm fires. Split from attached-object-secure, whose conjunct states no measure (0010). Who asserts it is named in § 107.49's lead-in, "Prior to flight, the remote pilot in command must:" (assertedBy, 0025).

entries.name: Certificate of waiver: issuance, and deviation under it
entries.evidence: (a) The Administrator may issue a certificate of waiver authorizing a deviation from any regulation specified in § 107.205 if the Administrator finds that a proposed small UAS operation can safely be conducted under the terms of that certificate of waiver. (b) A request for a certificate of waiver must contain a complete description of the proposed operation and justification that establishes that the operation can safely be conducted under the terms of a certificate of waiver. (c) The Administrator may prescribe additional limitations that the Administrator considers necessary. (d) A person who receives a certificate of waiver issued under this section: (1) May deviate from the regulations of this part to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver; and (2) Must comply with any conditions or limitations that are specified in the certificate of waiver.
entries.note: Out of scope: this map reads twelve sections of subpart B, and subpart E is not among them. It is an entry rather than an omission because rules inside the slice reach it: § 107.29(d) names certificates of waiver issued under § 107.200 (night-waiver-bar, night-waiver-termination), and § 107.205 lists the regulations a certificate issued pursuant to it may authorize deviation from (waivable-regulations, which (a) points at: "specified in § 107.205"). Nothing under the section is worked: whether to issue is the Administrator's finding under (a), and what a holder may do is "to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver" under (d), subject to conditions and limitations the certificate states and the corpus does not. The evidence is the whole section, which is short, so that the out-of-scope verdict covers the finding, the request, the additional limitations and the holder's deviation alike (#61, 0021).

entries.name: Regulations a certificate of waiver may authorize deviation from
entries.evidence: A certificate of waiver issued pursuant to § 107.200 may authorize a deviation from the following regulations of this part: (a) Section 107.25—Operation from a moving vehicle or aircraft. However, no waiver of this provision will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire. (b) Section 107.29(a)(2) and (b)—Anti-collision light required for operations at night and during periods of civil twilight. (c) Section 107.31—Visual line of sight aircraft operation. However, no waiver of this provision will be issued to allow the carriage of property of another by aircraft for compensation or hire. (d) Section 107.33—Visual observer. (e) Section 107.35—Operation of multiple small unmanned aircraft systems. (f) Section 107.37(a)—Yielding the right of way. (g) Section 107.39—Operation over people. (h) Section 107.41—Operation in certain airspace. (i) Section 107.51—Operating limitations for small unmanned aircraft. (j) Section 107.145—Operations over moving vehicles.
entries.note: Out of scope for the same reason as waiver-policy, and the gate every waivable rule in this map names in suspendedBy: a rule a certificate of waiver authorizes deviation from is unreachable while the waiver is held. The map records the edge and not the condition (0003); whether a waiver is held and what it authorizes deviation from is a fact about an instrument the Administrator issued, which the caller states and the engine never infers in either direction (0021). The edges follow the list paragraph by paragraph, judged by what each entry's locator states: (a) § 107.25 — moving-vehicle-operation, moving-aircraft-operation. (b) § 107.29(a)(2) and (b) — anti-collision-lighting, flash-rate-sufficient, intensity-reduction-in-interest-of-safety, and civil-twilight-operation, whose rule is (b) and whose (c) only fixes the term (b) uses. Not night-operation: § 107.29(a) as a whole is not listed, and under a lighting waiver (a)(1)'s training condition still applies, so the waiver reaches its lighting dependency and not the rule. Not night-training-completed ((a)(1)), night-waiver-bar or night-waiver-termination ((d)), civil-twilight-window or civil-twilight-alaska ((c)): none is listed. (c) § 107.31 — visual-line-of-sight, unaided-visual-contact. (d) § 107.33 — visual-observer-conditions, effective-communication, observer-coordination. (e) § 107.35 — single-aircraft. (f) § 107.37(a) — right-of-way, well-clear; not collision-hazard-proximity, which is (b). (g) § 107.39 — over-human-beings, direct-participation, reasonable-protection; not subpart-d-categories, which § 107.39(c) defers to and which is out of scope itself. (h) § 107.41 — airspace-authorized. (i) § 107.51, the whole section — speed-limit, altitude-limit, visibility-minimum, cloud-clearance, speed-within-limit, altitude-within-limit, weather-minimums-met, operating-limitations, prominent-objects; the values are included because the listed regulation is the section that states them. (j) § 107.145 is in subpart D, which subpart-d-categories declines as a whole; no in-scope entry states it, so (j) suspends nothing in scope, and its pointer resolves to that entry. Each other "Section 107.xx" pointer resolves to the entry at the level of the listed regulation: the whole section or paragraph, (b)'s lighting rule, and for § 107.51 the entry citing its introductory text, which reads over the section's paragraphs; "Section 107.25" is declared twice because no one entry states both of its limbs. The edges above reach further than those resolutions, to every entry inside the listed regulation. The provisos in (a) and (c) bound what the Administrator will issue, and are not evaluated. They mean a waiver of § 107.25 never lifts (b)'s "not transporting another person's property for compensation or hire", so the edge on moving-vehicle-operation reaches further than any waiver can. That costs a decline, not a wrong answer: a holder deviates only "to the extent specified in the certificate of waiver" (§ 107.200(d)(1)), and while the caller states a waiver is held the entry answers OutsideCurrentScope rather than a verdict. No suspended entry's own note repeats this judgement yet; it is recorded here, once.
